rows: A honeybee resolves detail only as fine as about a quarter of a grating cycle per degree, roughly one two-hundredth of what a person sees. Its middle is no sharper than its edge, so the picture stays soft all over.
A bee sees close to the whole way round, with a small blind region behind and below. The view is squeezed to fit a wide field.

Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, in ultraviolet, blue and green, so they see ultraviolet which people cannot. This view shows ultraviolet as blue, blue as green and green as red, and drops red, because bees do not see far red.
A bee sees flicker up to about 200 times a second in bright light, far faster than people. The view runs slower than yours to suggest that quicker sight.
A bee turns its head in quick jumps of 5 to 60 degrees, then holds its view still between jumps.
The glow, its colour, the gain, the speed-up and the wide soft ring are the app's own choices to make the bee's view easy to picture. No record gives these numbers.

rows: The two big front eyes each see a narrow upright strip, about 2 degrees wide and 21 degrees high. Everything the spider examines closely passes through this thin window.

In a typical species such as Phidippus johnsoni the receptors lie about 0.13 degrees apart, which gives about 3.8 cycles per degree. Portia fimbriata does far better, at about 12.5 cycles per degree, but this view uses the typical value.
Three pairs of smaller side eyes cover about 330 degrees in Trite planiceps and almost the whole circle in Metaphidippus. A small overlap of about 25 degrees lies straight ahead.
The side eyes see little detail. Their sharpness runs from about 0.3 to 1.3 cycles per degree, and the picture takes the middle of that range.

The side eyes behave as though blind to stationary things, and a light that only switches on and off starts no turn. A target must be wider than about 0.7 degrees and move about 1 degree to be seen. The front eyes spend longer looking at still or slowly moving images.

In most jumping spiders the front eyes carry two kinds of colour receptor. One peaks in the ultraviolet near 370 nm and one in the green near 530 nm. Some species have more, as Habronattus pyrrithrix has a third kind in the centre of its retina.

The front eyes sweep their retinas side to side across a target, one cycle every 1.1 to 1.3 seconds for small targets, and never less than 2 degrees wide. After the front eyes inspect a place, the side eyes withhold attention from that spot for about 5 seconds.

The app puts the strip in the middle of the picture, makes everything outside it fade unless it moves, and maps the two pigments to phone colours. It also draws the sweeping motion and the pause after a glance in its own way. Each of these drawings is the app's.

rows: Most scorpions have one pair of median eyes on top of the head and several pairs of smaller lateral eyes at the front corners. The buthid scorpions that were checked all have five pairs of lateral eyes.
Scorpions are reported to see through a full 360 degrees around the body. The two median eyes overlap by about 40 degrees above the animal.

The eyes of two scorpion genera respond most to blue (470 nm) and green (525 nm) light, and scorpion eyes are often described as most sensitive to green. This view shows the world in shades of a single green-sensitive channel.
Scorpions are nocturnal, and their eyes are sensitive to starlight levels of light. In one species the median eyes are about 1000 times more sensitive at night than by day.
The median eyes are the main eyes and give relatively high acuity and good spatial discrimination. The lateral eyes may only detect changes in light.

No one has measured how much detail a scorpion sees. This view assumes a soft picture and lifts the brightness a little for night. The choice of colour channel, and the way the circle is squeezed into the screen, are the app's.
Sand scorpions sense insects moving up to about 50 cm away through vibrations in the ground, and hairs on the pedipalps sense wind direction. The camera records neither.

Most octopus, squid and cuttlefish have a single visual pigment, with its peak between 470 and 500 nanometres. Tests on octopus and cuttlefish found no colour vision. The picture is drawn in grey.

One cuttlefish eye covers 253 degrees along the horizontal, and a young oval squid reaches 311 degrees at seven days old. A cuttlefish has about 86 degrees of overlap between its eyes at the front, and up to 75 degrees when it hunts.
An octopus pupil is round in darkness and closes to a horizontal slit in bright light. The slit appears in the first weeks after the young settle on the bottom.
An octopus has its most densely packed light receptors in a central horizontal stripe. A cuttlefish has a visual equator of high receptor density, set a little above the middle of the eye.
A squid follows flicker up to about 51 flashes a second. An octopus reaches 72 in very bright light and only 20 when the light is dim. A cuttlefish is put at 30. The picture keeps a person's pace.
An octopus can tell the plane of polarized light apart, and one test found a very small threshold. The picture leaves this out for now.

rows: A marmoset's cone mosaic could carry about 30 cycles per degree at the fovea, about what you manage. A stumptail macaque with an intact fovea resolved 1.4 minutes of arc, about 21 cycles per degree. We keep the sharpness at 30.

A grey mouse lemur resolves about 4.9 cycles per degree, and another estimate from its retina gives 4.2. A common marmoset has about half the acuity of a person. For a mouse lemur we blur the picture to 4.9.
Macaques have three kinds of cone, as you do. A cynomolgus monkey's cones are most sensitive near 430, 531 and 561 nanometres, so we colour the picture almost as you see it.

Male marmosets have two kinds of cone. Capuchins are two-cone or three-cone depending on the animal, and howler monkeys have three. The macaque's three cones stand for all of them, so some animals would see less colour than we show.
Owl monkeys are the only night-active monkeys. Their retinas have a single type of cone, so they lack colour vision, and their fovea is only rudimentary. We draw their view in grey.
A model built from chimpanzee and bonobo skulls gives a widest sideways reach of 115 degrees with the eye turned outward, against 136.1 degrees for a person. We scale a person's field by that ratio.

Neurons in a macaque's visual cortex respond to the small differences between the two eyes' pictures, which gives stereo depth. A marmoset can also focus over more than 20 dioptres. We leave depth as your camera gives it.

One value of sharpness stands for every monkey with a fovea, and one three-cone colour matrix stands for all primates. The chimpanzee field of view is worked out by scaling, and owl monkeys are drawn with no colour. No record gave a pupil shape, a dim-light gain or a field of view for other species, so those stay as a person's.

Bees see about 300 degrees around them on a level plane. In a honeybee each eye reaches 156 degrees back from straight ahead, which leaves only a small blind wedge behind.

Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, for ultraviolet, blue and green, with peaks near 346, 430 and 540 nanometres. They can see ultraviolet light but no far red. In this view ultraviolet appears as blue, blue as green and green as red, and red is dropped.

A honeybee can still follow flicker at about 200 times a second in bright light and 144 times a second at 300 lux. This view runs a little slowly to suggest an eye that catches more moments than ours.

Bees read the pattern of polarized light in the sky as a compass, using ultraviolet receptors in a special strip along the top of the eye and in their three small simple eyes. The faint overlay in this view is a picture of that sense.

rows: Retinal sharpness runs from about 1.6 cycles per degree in a manatee to 3.3 in a humpback whale and 4.8 in a Bryde's whale. A harbour seal reaches 11.5 under water. Yours is many times higher. We blur the picture to about 4.

Whales and seals that have been studied carry only one kind of cone, the long-wavelength kind, and lack the blue-sensitive kind, so they are essentially colour-blind. A dolphin's cone pigment peaks near 522 to 524 nanometres. We draw the picture with that single colour sensor. Manatees are the exception, with two kinds of cone.

Rorquals, right whales and sperm whales have lost the genes for both cone pigments, so their vision rests on rods alone. The rod pigment of a gray whale peaks at 492 nanometres and that of an elephant seal near 483, in the blue-green.

A bottlenose dolphin's two eyes together cover about 120 to 130 degrees, and the two views overlap in only 20 to 30 degrees. A sperm whale has the same panoramic field with no overlap. We squeeze the picture to 125 degrees.

A bottlenose dolphin sees 0.5 log units better than a person in dim light, which is about three times more light, and 0.2 log units worse in bright light. Many cetaceans and seals have a reflecting layer behind the retina, while manatees lack one. We brighten the picture about three times and add a faint sheen.

A bottlenose dolphin sends clicks between 40 and 150 kilohertz and can notice a change in echo delay as small as 1 microsecond. The sonar scene for small objects reaches about 100 metres. With the microphone on, this view can draw sound as rings across the picture.
A harbour seal can follow the wake of a fish for up to 30 seconds after it has passed, using whiskers that respond best between 10 and 100 hertz. No phone senses this, so it is left out.

The pick of 4 for sharpness, the 125 degree field, the single-sensor colour mapping, the threefold brightness gain, the sheen and the strength of the sound rings are the app's. The records cover many species that differ a good deal, so one view stands for all of them.

rows: Many monkeys and apes have three kinds of cone, as you do, but the owl monkey has a single kind and the bushbaby has one as well. Some New World monkeys vary between individuals. We show colour with a two-channel reading, which is the app's own choice.
A macaque or a stumptail macaque resolves about 21 to 30 cycles per degree, close to a person's 30. Marmosets and other small monkeys are set near 30 by cone counts. We blur the picture to about 12.
Owl monkeys and bushbabies are nocturnal. Owl monkeys have only a rudimentary fovea, and they lack colour vision, so their picture is grey with little sharp middle.
A Pan-like chimpanzee skull allows about 115 degrees of lateral field on one side. The app sets a whole-field figure of 180 degrees, a pick from that record.
The size of the sharp middle, the dim-light gain and the blend of colour are the app's guesses. No record gave them for these animals.

claims.how: Records give about 26.3, 21.4 and 30 cycles per degree; the app takes 12, below that range, as its own blur, so this is calculated and graded g.
The record gives 115 degrees of lateral field on one side; the app's whole-field pick of 180 is invented from that figure.
Records show three cone classes in many monkeys, one in owl monkeys and bushbabies, and variation in capuchins; the matrix here is the app's two-channel reading, not built from these records.

rows: A scorpion's eyes together see a full 360 degrees around the body. The median eyes take in a 40 degree overlap above the animal.

Scorpion eyes are most sensitive to green and blue light, with a second peak in the ultraviolet. Heterometrus and Tityus have measured peaks at 470 to 568 nm, and the lateral eyes respond to ultraviolet at 350 to 400 nm.
Scorpion eyes respond to starlight levels of light, and the lateral eyes of Androctonus australis detect differences in brightness at very low intensity. The picture is dim and built for night.

Scorpions sense the world mostly through slit sensilla and hairs on the legs and pedipalps, which pick up vibrations in sand and touch. Sand scorpions detect vibrations from prey as far as 50 cm away.

No record gives how much detail a scorpion sees. The app sets a coarse, dim picture with a faint green cast, a glow on movement, and a brightening so that night light reads. These are the app's choices.
Touch, vibration and airflow carry much of what a scorpion knows, and the camera records none of them.
